title: Why music
hookLine: raga is theology: the Word must be felt, not only read

lines: THE HARMONIUM, THE TABLA, A VOICE.
THROUGH THE EAR AND THE CHEST.
cards: The harmonium wheezes into its first note before anyone sings a word. Then the tabla comes in, soft at first, and a voice lifts a line from the Guru Granth Sahib, and the people sitting on the floor sing it back.
In the gurdwara, the hymns are sung. A visitor might wonder why. If the words are holy, why not just read them out clearly, so nobody misses a syllable?
The Sikh answer isn't that music makes the words prettier. It's closer to this: some things have to reach you through the ear and the chest before they reach the head.

teach.h: THE GRANTH IS ORDERED BY RAGA.
teach.b: First, look at how the book is built. After the opening prayers, the Granth is arranged by raga. Each hymn sits under a heading that names its musical mode before it names the Guru who wrote it.
The book is ordered like a songbook, by mood, not by date or author. A raga isn't just a tune. It's a mood, a color, a time of day, and the hymn was meant to arrive inside it.
Tradition says Guru Nanak traveled with a Muslim companion, Bhai Mardana, who played the rabab, a stringed instrument.
The janamsakhis, the old story collections, tell of Nanak asking Mardana to play, and the hymn coming as song. From the start, as Sikhs tell it, the Word came with music under it.
Third, the word for this singing: kirtan, singing the praise of God.
Guru Arjan, in Raag Maru, says that in this dark age kirtan is foremost. Not a decoration. Foremost.
You can read a line about longing and understand it. Sung in a raga made for longing, you meet it differently: in the breath, in the pause before the line comes back.
Many Sikh teachers speak of the Word needing to be felt, not only parsed. Music slows you to the hymn's speed. It makes you repeat.
It lets a room of strangers carry the same line together. A spoken sentence can slip past. A sung line comes around again.

how: In gurdwaras, the hymns of the Guru Granth Sahib are sung as kirtan, usually with harmonium and tabla, in the raga named at the head of each hymn, and the congregation often sings the refrain together.

o: because singing was the custom at royal courts
because music makes the hymns easier to memorize
because the Word is meant to be felt, not only read

p: the musical mood of a hymn

s: the Granth is arranged by author, one Guru after another
after the opening prayers it's arranged by raga, each hymn under its musical heading.
tradition pairs Guru Nanak with a musician, Bhai Mardana
tradition says Mardana played the rabab as the hymns came.

games.q: you're Guru Nanak on the road, and a hymn is coming to you. what do you ask your companion Mardana to do?
o: write it down so it isn't lost.
pick up the rabab and play.
stay quiet while you explain it.
games.why: the janamsakhis tell of Nanak asking Mardana to play, and the hymn arriving as song.

practice: If you can, play one recording of kirtan, any shabad, quietly; if you can't, just listen to the sounds around you.
Don't follow every word: let the sound land somewhere in your body, the chest, the throat, behind the eyes, and when a line comes back around, let it come back.
Hum along on one low, easy note if you'd like, and if you pray, let the listening be the prayer.

wordCard.voice: Why music. Because the Granth is a songbook ordered by raga, and kirtan, singing the praise, carries the Word into the body. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: kirtan, singing the hymns in praise of God.

carryVoice: Your line: felt, not just read. The book itself is a songbook. See you tomorrow.
